Missouri proposal would establish statewide child safety standards
Draft legislation would establish a uniform process for determining when children are unsafe and how authorities should intervene
Members of a child welfare task force established by Gov. Mike Kehoe gather on Nov. 5 to discuss draft legislation that would require child welfare workers, juvenile officers, judges and service providers to use a consistent child safety framework (Steph Quinn/Missouri Independent).
A Missouri child welfare task force has submitted draft legislation to Gov. Mike Kehoe that would define child safety in state law and require child welfare workers, judges and juvenile officers to follow a uniform process for identifying threats and determining when and how to intervene.
Kehoe created the 18-member task force by executive order in August, less than 24 hours before a bipartisan legislative committee held a hearing examining foster care deaths, child placements and turnover among frontline Children’s Division staff.
The proposed legislation describes the safety framework as a “sequential decision-making process” to identify safety threats, evaluate children’s vulnerabilities, assess a caregiver’s ability to protect a child and determine appropriate responses. Those could include community-based services, more structured intensive in-home services, temporary placements with relatives or longer-term removal from home.
Missouri lawmakers press child welfare leaders on foster care deaths, staff turnover
It’s similar to the safety assessment already used by Children’s Division investigators, called Structured Decision Making. That safety assessment was developed by the division and the Office of State Courts Administrator based on a guide published by the American Bar Association.
In an email to The Independent, Baylee Watts, media director for the Department of Social Services, said that while SDM is already the basis of initial safety assessments, “the broader, ongoing goal is to embed the safety framework throughout all practice areas — including when a child is in alternative care.”
The goal is to ensure that the reasons a child is considered unsafe — and what must change before that child can return home — are clearly described as the case moves through the child welfare system.
The legislation would require the division to establish the safety framework in state regulations and coordinate with the Office of State Courts Administrator to create standard forms for court reports and social service plans, as well as any other “uniform tools for the identification and evaluation of child safety.” The division would also develop training materials for juvenile and family courts, guardians ad litem, parents’ attorneys, law enforcement, medical professionals and child welfare agencies.
The legislation builds on efforts by division leadership to standardize child welfare practices statewide. Task force members said during the group’s Nov. 10 meeting that they plan to move forward with some changes, including developing standard forms, while lawmakers consider the legislation next year. Watts said the division also plans to begin promulgating rules needed to implement the proposed legislation.
Republican state Rep. Melissa Schmidt of Eldridge, who chairs the task force, has said throughout the group’s meetings that a shared framework and definitions will provide relief to overwhelmed division workers.

In a discussion on CNBC's Halftime Report Wednesday, the question came up: Why can't Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh hold the line on interest rates the way his icon Alan Greenspan did at the beginning of the dot-com era?
Greenspan famously leaned against inflation hawks on his committee in 1995 and 1996, holding the line on interest rates amid strong growth, because he believed in the productivity promise of the internet revolution.
It would be nice if Warsh could follow the same playbook amid the artificial intelligence build-out and keep rates steady until the productivity arrives. Unfortunately, a quick look at the numbers shows just how different the situation is for Warsh when it comes to inflation, the magnitude of the capital-investment boom and the monetary and fiscal stimulus boosting the economy.
Bottom line: the Fed looks like it has to hike — and maybe substantially — to be anywhere close to the position where the Fed was in Greenspan's time at the dawn of a major technological revolution.
Here are some key points:
- The nominal Fed funds rate was substantially higher in 1995 than it is today. The real, or inflation adjusted, funds rate was a positive 3.75% back then, and it's now at zero. So the Fed was leaning against the dotcom boom. Greenspan just decided not to lean more. Today, at a zero real rate, the Fed could be said to be fueling the boom.
- Inflation, as measured by the personal consumption expenditures price index, was substantially lower, right about target at 1.99% (even though there wasn't a formal 2% target then). It's above target now, at 3.8% according to government data published today, and going the wrong way.
- The current investment boom now is absolutely off the charts compared with the dot-com era. No real comparison. In 1995, spending on information processing equipment rose 15% year over year. In 2025, it was 27%. Looking at the latest data reported today, it grew 60% in the third quarter at an annualized rate. In the second quarter of 1995, it was 18%.
- Government deficit spending is substantially more stimulative now than it was then. In 1995, the deficit was just 2.2% of GDP. Today, it's 6.2%.
- Add higher oil prices, higher tariffs and the recent tax cuts and accelerated depreciation on investments, and there's a lot for the Fed to lean against.
It may be that the massive capex spending on AI will mean more productivity and less inflation down the road. Getting to the Philadelphia Marathon on November 22 proved an endurance event of its own for Travis Meier. The 38-year-old Minneapolis resident flew into Hartford, Connecticut, drove three hours into the Adirondack Mountains to pick up a canoe, then spent another five hours behind the wheel getting to Philadelphia. This was all before tackling Sunday’s 26.2 miles with the boat balanced over his head.
And yes, the canoe made it through the entire race without ever touching water.
“Coming from Minnesota, I can't just throw a boat in an overhead compartment," Meier told Runner's World. "It was a logistical nightmare: where to keep it, where to sneak it into the race, and how people would react to it."
Despite the travel headaches, Meier came away from Philadelphia with his second personal record in as many weeks. It was another step in his latest undertaking: 52 marathons in 52 weeks, each while carrying a canoe, to raise awareness about protecting the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness in northern Minnesota.
Meier, who manages a distillery when he isn't hauling boats around, wasn't exactly a seasoned runner when all this started. His introduction to the sport came through the Red Bull Urban Portage, an event that involved carrying a boat through downtown Minneapolis before paddling along the Mississippi River.
“I was really bad at paddling, but I could outrun people,” he recalled. Before the event, he bought a Northstar ADK canoe off Craigslist with every intention of selling it once the race was over. Instead, it found a home on his garage wall and managed to stick around for another year. Eventually, he started entering more races with it.
That eventually brought him to Minnesota's Ely Marathon in 2023, where he completed his first-ever 26.2-mile race while carrying a canoe. Since then, he's run only one conventional marathon without a boat, and what started solely as a personal experiment gradually became an opportunity to draw attention to a place he'd loved for years.
The Boundary Waters, a wilderness area known for its lakes, forests, and extensive canoe routes, has been at the center of a contentious debate over proposed mining operations. Federal protections restricting mining in the surrounding watershed were rolled back earlier this year, a development that particularly frustrated Meier.
"I've been to many remote places on this earth, and very few have its caliber of perfect,” he said. “So why would someone want to mess it up?"
A canoe as protest
Meier had been toying with the idea of running 52 marathons in 52 weeks ever since reading about Dane Rauschenberg, who accomplished the feat in 2006. With the ongoing fight over protections for the Boundary Waters, he had his reason to give it a shot, bringing his canoe as a form of protest to May’s Taco Bell 50K. It got people asking questions, which was exactly what he wanted, and gave him encouragement to keep showing up at races with a boat on his head.

Think this year's been a big one for data centers and their relentless power demands? Wait until you get a load of 2028.
A new report from Goldman Sachs Research estimates that the US will add about 52 gigawatts of data center power capacity in 2028 — nearly triple the 18 gigawatts expected this year and more than five times last year's additions. That's after data center power capacity and demand grew nearly 30% year over year so far in 2026, with data centers accounting for more than a third of all US power demand growth.
The forecast suggests that many of the issues associated with the AI boom — from rising electricity bills to competition for power and growing community opposition to data centers — could get considerably worse before the decade is out.
It's not just that tech companies are building more data centers. They're building bigger and more power-hungry ones. Goldman expects the average power capacity of a US data center building to reach 49 megawatts in 2028, up from 31 this year and 16 in 2020. The growth is also expected to be highly concentrated geographically. Virginia and Texas alone are projected to account for 36% of new US data center power capacity in 2028.
The projected growth in 2028 far exceeds the assumptions underpinning Goldman's existing natural gas outlook, which anticipates average annual data center power capacity additions of 28 gigawatts from 2027 through 2035. The analysts said the new estimates reinforced their bullish outlook for US natural gas prices through 2030.
But that growth isn't guaranteed. While Goldman's estimates already account for historical rates of project delays and cancellations, roughly half of the data center power capacity expected to come online in 2028 isn't yet under construction. The analysts warned that political changes following the midterm elections, as well as growing local opposition to data centers, could lead to more project delays and cancellations than expected.
In other words, the AI industry's appetite for power is growing just as political tolerance for that appetite is being tested.

A caller asked CNBC Mad Money's Jim Cramer in November whether to buy a stock near $140 or wait. Cramer thought the difference between paying $130 and $150 would look small on a chart 10 or 15 years later. Warren Buffett made a similar point in his 1996 shareholder letter. He looked for businesses he could understand, at prices he could justify, with earnings he expected to be substantially higher years later. Cramer has applied that thinking to entire industries. When investors soured on one corner of the market, he looked past the next quarter and pointed to developments he thought Wall Street was giving too little credit.
That approach puts the emphasis on what can sustain earnings. An aircraft engine can generate service revenue for years after delivery. A retailer that gains market share during a housing slump can capture more of the spending when buyers return. Both can be good businesses, but the price an investor pays determines how much of that future growth is already reflected in the shares. It is worth noting that when a parent asked how to invest $50,000 for a 12-year-old, Cramer put half in an index fund. He was more selective about what he'd buy with the other half.
The U.S. market's record shows what a longer holding period has historically done for diversified investors. From 1950 through 2025, the S&P 500's worst calendar-year total return was about −37%. Arizona State University finance professor Hendrik Bessembinder found that slightly more than 4% of U.S. stocks listed since 1926 accounted for all net shareholder wealth creation in his study.

Corporate Bonds vs. Dividend Stocks: Which Pays a Retiree More Reliably?
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Investment-grade corporate bonds are paying their highest yields in a year. Moody’s Seasoned Baa Corporate Bond Yield, a benchmark for the lowest tier of investment-grade debt, stood at 6.59%[1] in its October 1, 2026 monthly reading. That was the most recent figure available on November 25, 2026, and the 12-month high. For comparison, the 10-year Treasury yielded 4.92%[2] on November 23, 2026. Below, we line those rates up against two of the market’s most reliable dividend payers.
How a Corporate Bond Pays You and What Happens at Maturity
A corporate bond is a loan you make to a company. In return, the company promises a fixed interest payment, called the coupon, usually twice a year, and agrees to repay the bond’s face value on a set maturity date. The coupon is locked in when the bond is issued. The market yield changes every trading day, though, because the bond’s price moves.
When rates rise, existing bond prices fall; when rates drop, prices rise. A buyer today gets about the current market yield only by holding the bond to maturity, and only if the issuer pays in full. Some corporate bonds carry floating coupons that reset with short-term rates, so their income isn’t locked in.
Credit ratings from agencies like Moody’s and S&P measure the odds of getting paid, with investment grade running from the top AAA/Aaa tier down to BBB-/Baa3. Baa is the lowest rung before junk territory. The Baa series quoted above tracks bonds with maturities of 20 years and above[1]. Shorter bonds and higher-rated issuers generally yield less. Corporate bonds carry no FDIC insurance and no government guarantee, so if the issuer defaults, recovery depends on the company’s assets and where your bond ranks among its creditors. Even Treasuries, backed by the U.S. government, protect only principal and interest paid at maturity, and if you sell before then, the price can be lower than what you paid.
A bond fund works differently. It holds hundreds of bonds, never matures, and has a share price that moves with interest rates every day. Its monthly payout rises or falls as old bonds mature and the manager buys new ones at whatever rates the market offers. Individual bonds have their own version of that problem, called reinvestment risk. When a bond matures, or the issuer calls it early (which usually happens after rates fall), you have to reinvest at whatever rate is available then.

Warren Buffett and dividends are an old love story that continues to this day, as Berkshire'slatest 13F filing shows. The filing also reveals portfolio changes as CEO Greg Abel reshapes Berkshire's stock holdings after succeeding Buffett in January as the Omaha, Nebraska-based conglomerate's leader. Berkshire bought $2.37 billion worth of stocks in the third quarter and sold $2.79 billion. You can read about the fund's latest holdings here.
Dividend stocks continued to take center stage in the portfolio. Most of Berkshire's holdings are in companies that pay dividends, and many of them offer solid payouts. This has been an important part of Buffett's investment strategy over the years, and his successors at the firm appear to share that approach.
Analysts have long questioned why Berkshire Hathaway does not pay dividends to its own shareholders. Buffett has always been confident in his ability to put the company's capital to better use. He believes investing in businesses and other opportunities can generate better returns than distributing cash to shareholders. Even when he feels Berkshire cannot find attractive investment opportunities for its growing cash pile, he would rather return capital through share buybacks than dividends. In a 2018 interview with CNBC, Buffett explained his thinking: "Dividends have the implied promise that you keep paying them forever and not decrease them." He has also argued that repurchasing Berkshire's own shares can be more beneficial for shareholders.
In a 2023 report, The Wall Street Journal cited Todd Finkle, a professor of entrepreneurship at Gonzaga University and author of a book about Buffett's career. Finkle summed up Buffett's approach by saying, "That's what he loves: dividends and buybacks."
Finkle noted that Buffett has been particularly good at identifying businesses that can withstand different economic cycles while continuing to increase their dividends. These investments have helped grow the value of Berkshire's stock portfolio over time while bringing in cash that the company can use to support its businesses, make acquisitions, and buy back its own shares. For Buffett, dividends aren't "the secret sauce, but they're part of it," Finkle said. Given this backdrop, we will take a look at how much in estimated dividends Berkshire is expected to receive this year from some of its biggest holdings. Explore the full list here: How Warren Buffett Makes Billions from Dividend Stocks.

Our Methodology:
To estimate how much dividend income Berkshire Hathaway could collect from its stock portfolio in 2027, we reviewed the company's latest disclosed equity holdings and identified the stocks that pay regular dividends.
We then calculated the estimated annual dividend income from each holding by multiplying Berkshire's reported share count by the company's latest annualized dividend per share. For companies that pay quarterly dividends, we used the most recently declared quarterly payment multiplied by four.
We added the estimated income from each dividend-paying holding to arrive at Berkshire's projected dividend collection for 2027.
These figures are estimates, not guaranteed payments. These are estimates based on Berkshire's latest reported holdings and current dividend rates. Actual income may vary if Berkshire changes its positions or companies adjust their dividends.

Andreas Leal and his wife peruse the shelves at the Community Market, a food pantry operated by Cross-Lines Community Outreach in Kansas City, Kansas. Food banks and pantries across the country are experiencing surging demand amid declining federal food assistance and higher grocery prices. (Photo by Kevin Hardy/Stateline)
KANSAS CITY, Kan. — It doesn’t take long for the line to pile up at Cross-Lines Community Outreach as more people flock to the nonprofit food pantry to help stock their cupboards.
As the queue grew at the check-in counter two days before Thanksgiving, Andreas Leal and his wife perused the dwindling meat freezer and the hodgepodge of donated items on the toiletry shelves. A 75-year-old retiree, Leal said every bit helps when trying to keep up with rising prices.
“It’s very expensive,” he said. “Everything is expensive right now.”
Leal said his monthly Social Security benefit can’t keep up with rising costs. While the federal program boosted benefits by 2.8% this year, he said he just received notice that his residential property tax bill will jump 30%, costing him some $600. The increases require constant trade-offs. For example, to save on gas, the couple forgoes trips to visit their son who lives about 45 minutes away.
Leaders of Cross-Lines Community Outreach say such stories are more and more common. Its Community Market, a food pantry resembling a grocery store, serves about 1,900 families per month — a 35% increase over last year.
“Daily, we have to turn people away,” said Executive Director Susila Jones.
The market previously aimed to provide a couple pounds of frozen ground beef each month to every family. But those costs are now too high, pushing Cross-Lines to buy ground turkey or chicken — if prices are low enough.
Cross-Lines serves people across Wyandotte County, one of the most populous counties in Kansas with a poverty rate that exceeds state and national averages. In recent years, the food pantry has become more lenient about its income requirements and welcomed people who seek aid from multiple organizations.
“This is not what people want to do and so we really just let people come to us when they need to come to us,” she said. “Because we know even if you are working, if you’ve had steady income, just one paycheck can put you over the edge.”
Rising costs of groceries, housing and gas have pushed more people to seek emergency food assistance. At the same time, those charitable organizations are seeing a wave of Americans who have lost access to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, the nation’s largest food assistance program.
About 5.5 million Americans have lost SNAP benefits since last July’s passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which cut taxes and federal safety net programs. The law changed SNAP eligibility rules, ended certain work requirement exemptions and shifted new costs to states that administer the federal program.
More people are expected to lose SNAP aid as the legislation is fully implemented in the coming years. And earlier this month, the Trump administration proposed enrollment rule changes that would cut eligibility for another 6.3 million people.
Without congressional action, few experts see much relief ahead, further stressing the nation’s patchwork of churches, food banks and nonprofits laboring to keep people fed.

The state will provide a one-time list of sweetened beverages, candy and desserts that will be ineligible for purchase using federal food benefits starting Feb. 15. But grocers say they need a dynamic list to implement the changes consistently
The restrictions planned for Feb. 15 will impact the almost 5,000 retailers who are authorized to accept SNAP benefits in Missouri (Steph Quinn/Missouri Independent).
Missouri plans to give nearly 5,000 retailers a list of candy, sugary drinks and desserts that shoppers will no longer be able to purchase with federal food benefits starting Feb. 15. But grocers worry the list could quickly become outdated as products change.
To create the list, the Missouri Department of Social Services has received permission to forgo competitive bidding and make a one-time purchase of a Missouri-specific product database from global market research firm NielsenIQ.
The restrictions, approved by the federal government at the state’s request last year, will prohibit purchases of candy, prepackaged, shelf-stable desserts, sugary beverages and energy drinks through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP. They will also apply to a program called SUN Bucks that gives families of eligible children a one-time benefit of $120 to buy groceries during the summer.
The list is intended to help almost 5,000 SNAP retailers statewide implement the changes consistently, according to the department’s single feasible source purchase notice.
“Without this centralized procurement, approximately 4,944 SNAP-authorized Missouri retailers would each need to independently acquire the data, risking inconsistent implementation and federal noncompliance penalties,” according to the department posting.
But the Missouri Grocers Association, which advocates for the state’s grocery industry, says that unless the department provides regular updates to the list, retailers will struggle to implement SNAP restrictions uniformly as product formulations change and manufacturers release new products.
Dan Shaul, the association’s executive director, told The Independent he also worries retailers will be punished for inconsistencies that will be difficult to avoid.
“Yes, we’ll go ahead and program that list in,” Shaul said. “But then how do we make changes as our products change? I don’t think people understand the depth of product changes or (Universal Product Code) changes from retailer to retailer. Those things change constantly.”
Missouri’s plans are unfolding against the backdrop of federal court battles over the legality of SNAP restrictions in 23 states where the U.S. Department of Agriculture has approved waivers.
A class action lawsuit filed Nov. 18 and led by the National Center for Law and Economic Justice seeks to strike down proposed and current SNAP restrictions in 18 states, including Missouri, arguing federal officials lacked authority to use waivers to undertake such large-scale change to SNAP.
The lawsuit builds on the center’s ongoing legal challenge of SNAP restrictions in the five other states where USDA approved waivers. A judge blocked those waivers, in Colorado, Iowa, Tennessee and West Virginia in June, though the USDA has appealed the decision.

Pablo Hernández de Cos is set to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank next year.
He received backing from euro zone leaders at the European Council Summit, multiple media reported on Thursday.
The role still requires formal appointment after consultation with the European Parliament and the ECB's Governing Council, but neither has veto power and the decision follows intense political wrangling to reach a consensus on who should serve the eight-year term.
Reuters reported that de Cos was set for the nomination after the Netherlands agreed to back Klaas Knot, the only other candidate, citing European diplomatic sources.
De Cos is a 55-year-old economist and career central banker who rose through the ranks of the Bank of Spain, starting as a researcher in the 1990s and working in various departments before becoming governor from 2018 to June 2024.
He chaired the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision from 2019 to 2024, and has been General Manager of the Basel-based Bank for International Settlements since July 2025.
Both de Cos and his main rival for the ECB top job, Knot, were widely seen as candidates with deep knowledge and experience in monetary policy and financial stability — attributes that took on particular importance at a time of resurgent inflation, fragmentation and political uncertainty.
Lagarde had extensive experience in financial institutions but was criticized by some early in her tenure for a lack of central banking experience.
De Cos gained sufficient political backing in closed-door discussions and negotiations since Lagarde said she would step down on Feb. 7, 2027, over seven years after she became the first woman to helm the ECB. That was despite a final push by the Netherlands at the European Council meeting this week backing Knot.
Representatives from the euro area's biggest economies — Germany, France, Italy, Spain and the Netherlands — have been horse-trading as they look to secure representation on the central bank's six-member Executive Board.
Influential roles as chief economist, expected to go to Germany's Markus Brunnermeier, and head of the Markets Portfolio, for which France's Laurence Boone has reportedly been tapped, also change hands in 2027.
Not a dove, not a hawk, but an 'owl'
Analysts say de Cos's commentary and actions over more than two decades at Spain's central bank paint him as moderately dovish — inclined to favor lower interest rates to support economic growth — but also as a pragmatist who has been willing to adapt.
That has included support for strong rate hikes during the energy price shock that followed Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, but also giving staunch backing for rates below zero and the huge stimulus package launched by then-ECB President Mario Draghi to reboot the euro zone economy in 2019.
De Cos quipped in 2024 that he was an "owl" after being asked if he was a hawk or a dove, emphasizing his focus on data and the situation at hand.
"It is true that Hernández de Cos supported the ECB's uber-dovish monetary policy during the period when inflation was persistently below target. However, his monetary policy views may well be regime-dependent," Christian Kopf, head of fixed income and foreign exchange at Union Investment, said in emailed comments.

The Trump administration has unveiled a fresh tariff salvo on more than a dozen trading partners, with China, Vietnam, and India facing some of the steepest potential rates and mounting pressure to conclude trade deals with Washington.
The proposed tariffs, framed as curbing excess industrial capacity, start at 15% for the European Union, South Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan and rise to as much as 35% for Vietnam.
The U.S. Trade Representative's Office said it intends to cap the new duties at lower levels for countries that have completed trade deals or are still negotiating with Washington.
The overall impact on the region is likely to be limited, said Mark Williams, chief Asia economist at Capital Economics. The proposal "puts most of the targeted countries back where they were earlier in the year," he said, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's emergency tariffs in February.
Still, the proposal could give some countries an incentive to speed up trade talks in order to lock in lower tariff rates, analysts said.
On Wednesday, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said that the new policy likely will not take effect for months, with a senior U.S. official saying the duties could take effect as early as January.
China
China faces a capped rate of 20%, on top of an existing 25% tariff imposed during President Donald Trump's first term. The rate could rise to 40% if the trade truce reached in South Korea last October is not extended beyond January, the USTR said.
Beijing has rejected Washington's claim of excess capacity while vowing to take measures necessary to protect its rights.
On Thursday, Chinese Commerce Ministry spokesperson He Yadong called on Washington to "rectify its wrongdoing and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue."
He was responding to Washington's plan to raise tariffs following its Section 301 investigations, while the ministry also urged the U.S. to implement $30 billion of reciprocal tariff cuts agreed by the two sides in late September.

The brand’s arrival in trail running seems genuinely seamless and expected. My impressions of all the shoes are that they are solid, not only in their reliability and capability, but also in their value. The shoe has an actual weight of 10.4 ounces (294 grams) for a U.S. men’s 9, compared to 9.2 ounces (260 grams) for the Venosk and 9.6 ounces (271 grams) for the Vezor. The upper is protective. The midsole provides firm comfort with extra energy and forgiveness coming from the insoles and protection from a shield plate. The DuraGrip Ultra outsole with 4-millimeter lugs faced the summer and fall terrain with aplomb.

The Benefits of This Workout for Runners
“I chose to focus on areas where traditional endurance athletes may have weaknesses due to underutilization,” Miklaus tells Runner’s World. Because running and most of our daily movements occur in the sagittal plane of motion—that’s forward and backward—we tend to neglect muscles used in lateral (or side-to-side) and rotational movements, causing weakness in these areas. While that not only leads to suboptimal performance, it can also increase your risk of injury, he explains.
“By implementing a lower-body routine that incorporates lateral and rotational movements, as well as upper-body and core training, runners can increase their overall athletic standards and the functional capacity of their bodies,” Miklaus says.
In addition to making you move in different planes of motion, this workout also alternates lower-body and upper-body or core exercises. That way, one muscle group gets rest as the other works, Miklaus explains, without you having to take much actual rest time.
The lower-body moves also get more difficult as you work through the seven-exercise circuit, while the upper-body ones become less intense. “This is intended to provide a balanced challenge and allow each athlete space to scale the difficulty [of the workout] to their own fitness level,” Miklaus explains.
How to do the workout: Do each exercise in order for 45 seconds. Rest for 15 seconds while also transitioning into the next move. Repeat for four total sets.

Wells Fargo Is Now the Largest Institutional Holder of Spot Bitcoin ETFs. If Banks Are Buying Bitcoin, Should You?
Wells Fargo owns a ton of the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF, but that’s not as instructive as some investors may think.
By Todd Shriber –
Key Points
- Wells Fargo’s third-quarter 13F reveals the bank more than doubled its position in the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF.
- As of the end of September, the bank owned nearly $2.4 billion worth of the Bitcoin ETF.
- That doesn’t mean investors should follow suit.
It is Form 13F filing season, meaning it's a good time to bone up on exactly what that regulatory document is. The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) requires that investors exercising "investment discretion over $100 million or more" reveal their holdings in Form 13F within 45 days of the end of the prior quarter.
Likely due in part to some investors' reverence for Warren Buffett, among other famous professional market participants, following 13F filings is something of a sport. However, it's not always the best way to track what the smart money is doing.
Wells Fargo increased its holdings of the iShares Bitcoin Trust, but that’s not a buy signal. Image source: Getty Images.
Take the case of Wells Fargo (WFC -0.31%) and the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT +0.92%), the largest spot Bitcoin (BTC +4.02%) exchange-traded fund (ETF).
There's a 'but'
Third-quarter 13F filings indicate that several banks, including Wells Fargo, increased exposure to various spot Bitcoin ETFs. On the surface, that may be all some investors need to know before grabbing for the falling knife (hopefully a temporary condition) that is the world's largest cryptocurrency.
Indeed, Wells Fargo more than doubled its holdings of the iShares Bitcoin Trust to nearly 49.6 million, worth about $2.4 billion, as of the end of the third quarter. Investors need to dig deeper than that. Here's why: roughly 85% of the bank's position in the king of Bitcoin ETFs is held on behalf of brokerage clients.
Put another way, the bulk of Wells Fargo's stake in the Bitcoin ETF is attributable to folks who trade on the bank's platform or to clients of Wells Fargo Advisors – the bank's wealth management arm. That means that the bank, for the most part, is NOT directly making a directional bet on the iShares ETFs. It's merely taking custody of the fund on behalf of its customers who own it.

Wells Fargo's involvement with the Bitcoin ETF isn't comparable to, say, Berkshire Hathaway revealing a new position or adding to an existing holding. News to that effect often boosts the stock in question because Berkshire is making a clear bullish bet. That's simply not the case with Wells Fargo and this Bitcoin ETF.
Hope for HODLers
Bitcoin bulls (sometimes known in crypto lingo as HODLers) who are disappointed by the revelation that Wells Fargo's big boost to its Bitcoin ETF position means little can take heart, as there are some encouraging signs in other 13Fs. P&G can offset some of this pressure through its scale, which gives it bargaining power with suppliers and retailers, and through its cost-cutting programs.
The stock trades at about 25 times this fiscal year's earnings estimates, and analysts expect earnings to grow about 4.7% annually. That's not a bargain valuation, but it's a reasonable price for a business that keeps growing and returning a growing cash payout to shareholders year after year.
